title: Gesture: Hand Pose Into Command
description: A wave, a thumbs up, an open palm — turning a hand's shape into an instruction ARIA can act on.

content.value: Detecting the Hand, Then Reading It

Gesture recognition is a two-step version of the same idea from the last two lessons. First, detect where a hand is and the position of its key points — fingertips, knuckles, wrist — the same box-and-landmark technique as face detection. Then, a second step matches that pattern of points against a small library of known gestures.

content.title: 🔎 Detect the hand pose
content.hint: The hand is detected first — matching it to a specific gesture is the next step.

content.value: Once the key points are known, matching them to a gesture is closer to Module 9's decision blocks than to detection: an open palm's fingertips are all far from the wrist; a fist's are all close to it. A small set of rules — or a trained pattern, either approach works — turns that geometry into a name: "stop", "come here", "turn around".

detected hand landmarks --> measure fingertip-to-wrist distances
                        --> match against known gesture patterns
                        --> command: "stop" / "come here" / "wave back"

This is exactly the sense-think-act loop again, just with a much richer sense step. "Command detected" is the THINK output; what ARIA does with that command — stopping, approaching, waving — is still an ordinary ACT step, no different from anything earlier in this course.

Key takeaway: gesture recognition detects a hand's key points, then matches their geometry against known gesture patterns to produce a command — a richer SENSE step feeding the exact same loop this whole course has been building.

quiz.question: What are the two steps behind gesture recognition?
options: Detect the hand and its key points, then match that pattern against known gestures
Just one step — gestures are detected directly with no intermediate stage
Reading the person's voice, then their hand
quiz.explain: Detection finds the geometry; a separate matching step turns that geometry into a named gesture.

quiz.question: How does an open palm's landmark geometry typically differ from a closed fist's?
options: There's no measurable difference at all
An open palm's fingertips sit far from the wrist; a fist's sit close to it
Fists have more visible landmarks than open palms
quiz.explain: That distance measurement is exactly the kind of simple geometric feature a gesture-matching step can use.

quiz.question: How does gesture recognition fit the sense-think-act loop from Module 1?
options: It doesn't fit that loop at all — gestures are a completely separate idea
It's a richer SENSE step; the resulting command still becomes an ordinary THINK/ACT sequence
It replaces the THINK step entirely
quiz.explain: Detecting and naming a gesture is still just sensing, in the end — everything the robot does with that command is the same THINK/ACT this course has always used.
